## Design

### 2026-10-07 – I spent the first 3 hours learning how to use KiCad, specifically it's schematic editor. I followed a tutorial on building a beginner project, and learned how to use the editor along the way. The desi

**13h**

I spent the first 3 hours learning how to use KiCad, specifically it's schematic editor. I followed a tutorial on building a beginner project, and learned how to use the editor along the way. The design in the image (which is the project from the tutorial) is based on the LM555 timer, which can blink a LED with a frequency that can be adjusted by the trimmer. This project let me understand the basics of making circuits, such as GND, Resistors, mounting holes, power sources, etc.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/92001df3a5e7cfe88d9c44cd0f61cb4f5d9b59b5694b894f7e1c59de59c8d22b.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/a550f53c55ac21b4fa28d968835f6333346e553343e63b5b42adaf584dec07b4.png)

I then spent the remaining 10 hours drafting a full PDF for the SkyEar Project. The document includes a detailed parts list, the overall design of SkyEar, and small diagrams to help me understand how each section of the circuit connects together before I start drawing the final schematic.

SkyEar is divided into seven main blocks: power, virtual ground (VREF), antenna buffer, hum filter, gain stage, high-frequency filter, and outputs. Breaking the project into these blocks helped me understand the purpose of each part of the circuit instead of treating the entire schematic as one complicated design.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/1a6a78791dbfe91f6d905e86067e090d29207777682ec215a8b47edaf00e8cc9.png)

### 2026-10-11 – This session was all about getting SkyEar's complete schematic into KiCad, which is the core of my Week 1 PCB design. Since my build guide already had every part, value and connection worked out block

**15h**

This session was all about getting SkyEar's complete schematic into KiCad, which is the core of my Week 1 PCB design. Since my build guide already had every part, value and connection worked out block by block, I made the KiCad schematic directly from it. It came out as a single sheet with 52 parts, split into labeled sections that follow the signal from the antenna all the way to the headphones, and every part already has a real KiCad footprint assigned so it's ready for the PCB editor.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/ba91c17436d243cf8981e67b279e908506f42c66fc3a1f47a9b0805a25a25caa.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/9cf20ff45d09b46a24aec66c60421bfd0f2d6fc3d3188eab844d11bbf0903134.png)

The power section takes a 9 V battery through a screw terminal (J1) and a slide switch (SW1), then through a 1N5817 Schottky diode (D1). The diode means plugging the battery in backwards can't fry anything, and I picked a Schottky because it only drops about 0.3 V instead of 0.7 V like a normal diode. C1 (100 µF) and C2 (100 nF) smooth out the supply, and a 4.7k resistor feeds a power LED at about 1.5 mA. Next to it is the virtual ground: two 10k resistors split the battery in half to make a ~4.35 V "VREF", with C3 and C4 keeping it quiet. Audio signals swing both above and below zero, but a single battery only gives 0 V and +9 V, so every op-amp signal swings around VREF instead.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/e886a0ec390ff00cfebcf3c1fa459604a6da6f1d528747fc0f261273c7ab0b6f.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/02953ceb994f48cd71fb1ec1cf44874eaf5430df0b1d91a8fb79f793d879fa6d.png)

The antenna input was the most interesting part to understand. A short wire antenna behaves like a tiny ~30 pF capacitor, so it can barely push any current. That's why R5 is 10 MΩ instead of a normal 10k, and why the first stage (U1A, half of a TL072) is a buffer that just copies the signal without loading it. The TL072 has JFET inputs, which is what lets it handle such a high resistance. R5 and the antenna capacitance also form the first filter, starting to cut hum below ~530 Hz. R4 and two 1N4148 diodes (D3, D4) protect the input by dumping static from the antenna into the power rails. C5 is marked "do not fit" and only gets soldered if I end up hearing AM radio.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/1b496b166d11c9f8e4b794a4f7f1a9524457f419218260c267ee57d343f77c8a.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/74ddeefe6a4ea79f2ec9985e5d6e00f72850c6060d0b16c362d6bce9292bf2ac.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/45f83cab021dcf6388a3ceca7a31eb668ea85315e6ce030d65863f5b472f6543.png)

After the buffer comes the hum filter (U1B), a 2nd-order high-pass at about 625 Hz built from two 10 nF caps, an 18k and a 36k. Making the 36k exactly twice the 18k gives a flat Butterworth response with no bump at the cutoff. Power lines put out 60 Hz hum that's thousands of times stronger than lightning on another continent, so this filter is what makes the whole thing usable. Then U2A amplifies the signal by 1 + 100k/3.3k ≈ 31. C9 keeps DC from getting amplified so the output stays centered on VREF, and C8 (150 pF) starts rolling off the highs. U2B is a 2nd-order low-pass at ~10.7 kHz that cuts hiss, AM radio, and the Navy's huge VLF transmitters around 20 to 25 kHz, which could otherwise overload everything.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/17ddcda4d360590bcd450767719f514ba99f5120bea9faf485ea730dcfe12e6e.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/139cb37ac0083989316fe2d5152dace6214eca332bf1455320043c6e6105f3c2.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/1fd032894d20e4eb8b66421ed5b4a4654681c78ec8622dc7241a513bb86dc32b.png)

The output splits two ways. The line out (J4) goes through a 10 µF cap and a 1k resistor so I can record the audio or feed it into my later Half Life projects. The headphone path goes through a 10k audio-taper volume knob (RV1) into an LM386 amp that adds another x20, so the total gain from antenna to ears is around 620. R14 and C17 (10 Ω + 47 nF) keep the LM386 from oscillating, C18 (220 µF) blocks DC from reaching my headphones, and R15 (47 Ω) caps the maximum volume so it can't blast my ears. Tip and ring on the jack are tied together so the mono signal goes to both ears.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/40b1fa6d2f36e3efee876ca3ef0a32a92db7a0655c59ce229316d67d906625f1.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/a6614b7c994dcaa8296a67dd1f15507e8938f370a7bd9d183ed6a8b9f8083461.png)

For checking, the schematic passed KiCad's Electrical Rules Checker with 0 errors, every one of the 27 nets was compared against my guide, every footprint's pads were matched to its symbol's pins (the headphone jack's T/R/S pads were the one I was most worried about), and every electrolytic cap was checked to have its + side on the higher voltage. The project file also already has my track widths set: 0.6 mm for +9V and GND, and 0.3 mm for signals. ![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/9849dbd3d263cf17988f9b0a165751ed1b4c9a8c09ea209b6cbf5c7158856708.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/MKgCk7zGSEGyPKVHotrzwyfhpTbuYweh/0223866f31266de5134ba6e8d59d48484047e2cc4b6d33e1ee5c851abdaf3644.png)

One thing I still need to figure out is the budget. Tier 1 is $30 and my rough estimate is $35 to $50 once the PCB and the antenna are included, so my next step is pricing the real BOM. After that comes the PCB layout, where the main rule is keeping the antenna input as far as possible from the headphone amp so the loud output can't leak back into the input and squeal.
